title: the Sama Veda as song
hook: a poem on a page and the same poem sung are not the same thing. the Sama Veda takes hymn verses and gives them a tune

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna with their goodbye: you all, protect us always with well-being. Did you mean a goodbye when you said one? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

Read a song lyric off a screen, flat, with no tune. Something's missing. The words are all there, every one, and yet the line just sits on the page. Now hear the same line sung. It stretches where it wants to. A short word holds for three beats. A syllable climbs and falls. Nothing about the words changed, and everything about them changed. This week we've been reading the Rig Veda's hymns as words: to Agni, to Indra, to Ushas, to Varuna. Hindu tradition keeps another Veda that takes verses like these and does what a melody does to a lyric. Today: the Sama Veda, the Veda as song.
screen: `A LYRIC READ FLAT.` → `THE SAME LINE, SUNG.` → `THE VEDA AS SONG.`

segments.voice: The word saman means a chant, a melody. The Sama Veda is the Veda of those melodies. Here's the surprise: it doesn't bring a new set of words. Its verses are ones that also appear in the Rig Veda, from hymns like the ones we've been hearing all week, gathered and set to tune. So the Sama Veda isn't a second set of lyrics. It's the music. Listen to where it begins. Its opening verse is a call to the fire: agna a yahi vitaye. Come, Agni, to the feast. The same Agni whose hymns opened the Rig Veda opens the songbook too. The words are an invitation, and in the Sama Veda the invitation is sung. Why would a tradition keep a whole Veda of melody? Because in the old rites, different priests had different jobs. Some recited the verses. Some sang them. The Sama Veda belongs to the singers. Their task wasn't to say what the hymn means. It was to carry it on a voice that rises, holds and falls, so the words don't just land. They ring. Tradition treats the melody itself as sacred, not decoration added later, and the chants were handed on from teacher to student by ear. On an ordinary day this is easy to test. Say good morning to someone flatly. Then say it as if you're glad they're here. Same two words. The tune is part of what you said.
screen: `SAMAN: A CHANT, A MELODY.` · `RIG VEDA VERSES, SET TO TUNE.` · `IT OPENS: COME, AGNI, TO THE FEAST.` · `THE TUNE IS PART OF WHAT IS SAID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a sound carry your breath. Sit comfortably. Breathe in through the nose. On the out-breath, hum, quietly, one low steady note, and let it last as long as the breath does. Feel where it buzzes: lips, nose, chest. Breathe in again, and hum again. Don't make a tune. Just let the voice ride the breath out. If humming isn't possible where you are, hum without sound and feel the breath alone. If you pray, you can let one hum be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Sama Veda as song. Saman, melody: verses from the Rig Veda's hymns, set to tune and sung. Today's word.
screen: `THE SAMA VEDA AS SONG — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Sama Veda as song. Today, say one ordinary sentence as if it were worth singing, a thank you, a good morning, a name. Notice what the tune adds. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

notes: Claim that the Sama Veda's verses 'mostly' also appear in the Rig Veda is a quantity claim beyond any cited text; it is the standard description, but a Keeper should confirm or soften to 'its verses also appear in the Rig Veda'. The myth item and trapdoor ('largely') rely on it.
Opening verse of the Sama Veda: agna ā yāhi vītaye gṛṇāno havyadātaye (also Rig Veda 6.16.10); confirm reference and the gloss 'come, Agni, to the feast' (vītaye, 'for the meal/enjoyment').
'Some recited the verses. Some sang them. The Sama Veda belongs to the singers' refers to the division of priestly roles (hotṛ, udgātṛ); confirm the simplification.
Week-end review covers days 1268–1273 (fire, storm, dawn, order); days 1268–1271 were written by another writer.
Devanagari सामन् (stem form); some prefer साम. Confirm.
